articles.title: 4 Domain Registrars, Ranked by Renewal Price (October 2026)
articles.excerpt: Here's something nobody tells you when you buy your first domain: the price on the homepage is a lie. Not technically — it's the real first-year price. But it's not the price you'll pay. The price you…
articles.body: Here's something nobody tells you when you buy your first domain: the price on the homepage is a lie. Not technically — it's the real first-year price. But it's not the price you'll pay. The price you'll actually pay, year after year, is the renewal price, and it's usually buried three clicks deep in a pricing page nobody reads. I went down this rabbit hole because I was auditing my own domain bills. I own a handful of domains across different registrars, and when I lined up what I was actually paying per year, the numbers didn't match what I remembered paying. So I pulled the real renewal prices for the four registrars developers actually use, and the gap is kind of wild. Everything below is researched from the registrars' own published pricing pages as of October 2026.
articles.author: Paul Lovelace

articles.title: Ollama v1 OpenAI Compat Drops Think Toggle
articles.excerpt: The Problem We recently ran into an issue with the Ollama /v1 endpoint, which is designed to be compatible with OpenAI's API. Our models, particularly those from the Qwen3 family, were returning empty…
articles.body: The Problem We recently ran into an issue with the Ollama /v1 endpoint, which is designed to be compatible with OpenAI's API. Our models, particularly those from the Qwen3 family, were returning empty content. This was not the behavior we expected, given the models' capabilities. What We Noticed We started by examining the requests and responses to identify what was going wrong. We noticed that the /v1 endpoint was silently dropping the think: false toggle for the Qwen3-family models. This toggle is crucial as it controls whether the model spends its entire num_predict budget on internal reasoning or not.

articles.title: More users or clearer feedback: which product should you keep building?
articles.excerpt: One product has more users, but the feedback is mostly "looks useful." The other has fewer users. But a few are willing to show you how they use it and try your next update. You only have time to focu…
articles.body: One product has more users, but the feedback is mostly "looks useful." The other has fewer users. But a few are willing to show you how they use it and try your next update. You only have time to focus on one this month. The usual answer is to pick the one with users already asking for changes. Or the one with the larger market, stronger technology, or the shortest path to launch. Those comparisons still matter. But they don't tell you how hard it will be to keep improving after launch. On Hacker News, a founder was deciding which of four tools to open-source first. Two were already built, and one was getting some users through ChatGPT. The founder said they weren't talking to enough customers, and improvements were coming slowly after the initial build.

articles.title: My job search API taught me that salary fields are a lie told in three currencies
articles.excerpt: I built a job postings search API so my agent could monitor the market for interesting roles without scraping job boards. The schema looked clean: title, company, location, salary, description. One ca…
articles.body: I built a job postings search API so my agent could monitor the market for interesting roles without scraping job boards. The schema looked clean: title, company, location, salary, description. One call, structured data. Then I started actually reading the salary fields. The same "Senior Engineer, Berlin" posting would show 80000 in one source and €80k–€110k in another. Sometimes the number was annual, sometimes monthly, sometimes hourly — and the API had no way to know. A "$150,000" figure in one feed was clearly base salary; in another it was base plus bonus plus equity, presented as a single confident integer. Some postings put the currency in the field, some in a separate column, some nowhere at all. The worst case: a "120000" with no currency and no period. Is that pounds? Euros?
articles.author: InApp

articles.title: One AI agent taught another a trick through my orchestrator. It didn't help, and the orchestrator noticed
articles.excerpt: Three days ago I wrote about giving AI agents a harm budget instead of trust. All of it was a sandbox. Fake shop, fake customers, fake money. A few of you asked the fair question. Does any of this wor…
articles.body: Three days ago I wrote about giving AI agents a harm budget instead of trust. All of it was a sandbox. Fake shop, fake customers, fake money. A few of you asked the fair question. Does any of this work outside the sandbox? So I took the part I was proudest of, agents learning from each other's verified experience, and tried it on a real task with real websites and a real model. It took three attempts. The short version is that the transfer itself works now, the trick didn't help, and the orchestrator refused to approve it. Getting to an honest "it didn't help" was the interesting part. At the end there's a list of everything that changed since the first post. Most of it came from your comments.

articles.body: TL;DR Google Search’s AI Mode no longer offers the direct “Export to Docs” shortcut in its three-dot menu. Gemini and NotebookLM still offer Docs export options, but Google hasn’t explained whether AI Mode’s shortcut will return. Imagine researching a complicated topic with Google Search AI Mode , gathering explanations and useful information, then saving everything to Google Docs for later. Until recently, that last step took just a couple of taps. But Google appears to have quietly removed the shortcut from Search, frustrating users who relied on it to turn their searches into editable documents.

articles.title: Australia's bizarre 'Spider Crater' seen from orbit | Space photo of the day for Oct. 22, 2026
articles.excerpt: A satellite image of "Spider Crater" in Western Australia.
articles.body: A satellite image of "Spider Crater" in Western Australia. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey ) From the dangerous Sydney funnel-web to the common huntsman, Australia is home to its fair share of spiders. It even has a crater shaped like one. What is it? One stretch of the vast Western Australia wilderness is imprinted with a curious crater, which likely formed after a meteor impact hundreds of millions of years ago. Geologists think the spider-like pattern in the crater's center was created when its floor rebounded following the initial impact, NASA has said . In the hundreds of millions of years since the initial impact, erosion has continued to carve this formation into its current, signature shape.

"The update will include details about NASA’s Artemis III mission that will send four astronauts to low Earth orbit next year to test critical systems needed for future lunar landings, and how plans to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028 are progressing," NASA officials said in an Oct. 14 media advisory . The crew of NASA's Artemis II mission captured this photo of a crescent Earth on April 6, 2026, as they began passing behind the moon.

articles.title: Faster to Science: A Letter to the Science Community
articles.excerpt: NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall.
articles.body: Dear NASA Science Community, NASA Science wants to deliver science faster, so we’re changing how we compete and select missions. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall, from NASA Headquarters, to explain our new Competition Model 2.0 (CM 2.0), and answer your questions. ( Details below. ) We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long. It has taken years to move mission concepts through the current two-step process. This has often come with contract management challenges, unpredictability, and not enough funding. NASA is committed to doing better — and I’m excited to share with you how we’re making it happen.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year.
